title: RAG Anatomy: Why Retrieve
objective: After this lesson you will be able to explain RAG's three reasons (freshness, grounding, cost), map the ten-stage pipeline, and decide RAG vs fine-tuning vs bigger prompts per use case.
why: Language models freeze knowledge at training, invent specifics under uncertainty, and charge per token for everything pasted. RAG (retrieval-augmented generation) answers all three: live data retrieved per query, claims bound to sources, compact relevant context instead of whole manuals. It is the architecture behind every serious store assistant, support copilot, and doc Q&A system — and this course builds it on product data.

blocks.text: **Freshness**: prices, policies, and inventory change hourly — retrieval reads current rows, no retraining. **Grounding**: answers cite spans, converting hallucinations into checkable claims or visible abstentions. **Cost**: retrieving 5 chunks beats pasting manuals and beats fine-tuning runs. Each reason maps to a failure it prevents: staleness, invention, and budget blowout.
RAG vs fine-tuning vs bigger prompts

**Bigger prompts** (paste everything): dies on scale, cost, and staleness — prototyping only. **Fine-tuning**: bakes stable behavior/style/reasoning patterns; useless for changing facts, uncitable by construction. **RAG**: live facts with sources; needs retrieval quality work. Production reality combines: tuned behavior over retrieved facts, with prompts structuring both.

blocks.title: Route the need
blocks.note: Run it: expect 4/4. Architecture choice is a decision procedure over need properties (freshness, citability, stability) — not loyalty to any technique.

items: RAG for fresh/grounded/affordable facts; fine-tuning for stable style/skills; big prompts for prototypes
Ten stages from ingest to evaluate — each lesson owns stages, failures localize by stage
Route architectures by need properties, never by hype

exercise.prompt: (a) Run the practice router and confirm 4/4. (b) Classify five store needs (hourly prices, brand voice, cited returns policy, size advice, full-manual Q&A) with one-line reasons. (c) State which two stages your current project would most likely fail at, and what evidence would prove it.
hints: 4/4 baseline; each case exercises one decision rule (fresh/cite → RAG; stable style/skill → tune/prompt; small static → paste).
Prices→RAG; voice→tune/prompt; cited policy→RAG; size advice→RAG over size charts (fresh-ish, citable); manual→RAG.
Honest picks with proofs: chunking (hit-rate on gold) or grounding (citation audit) — failures need named evidence, not vibes.
exercise.why: Architecture routing plus self-assessment (weakest stages with proofs) are the two strategic skills: choose rightly, then aim improvement where evidence points.

quiz.q: Hourly-changing prices with citations required. Architecture?
options: RAG: live reads + citable spans; fine-tuning freezes and can't cite
quiz.explain: Freshness + grounding jointly force RAG. Fine-tuning serves stable behavior, never live facts.

quiz.q: RAG pipeline fails. How do you localize?
options: Per-stage checks: chunks exist? retrieval hits? rerank orders? generation cites? — stage-wise evidence isolates
quiz.explain: Pipelines debug stage by stage with each stage's metric. Blanket fixes waste effort on healthy stages.

quiz.q: When is pasting the whole manual acceptable?
options: Prototypes and tiny static corpora only — scale, cost, and staleness kill it in production
quiz.explain: Dumps work until tokens, money, or freshness object. Production needs retrieval; prototypes need speed.

summary: Fresh, grounded, cheap — RAG's three reasons with a ten-stage pipeline and need-based architecture routing. Every later lesson owns stages of this map.
next: Pipeline mapped — now its first material: chunking product catalogs into retrievable, citable, metadata-rich units. Next: units that answer.
